newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sorghum quiet, cotton looks good-Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australia sorghum quiet, cotton looks good-Grainco.

text.p: Australia's sorghum market remains relatively subdued although late last week the export market lost some ground on lower wheat values and favourable planting conditions in the United States, Queensland grains co-operative Grainco Ltd said in its weekly market report.
Harvest was virtually over in southern Queensland while the early harvest was beginning in central Queensland, trading manager Rob Brealey said.

The domestic market in southern Queensland continues to trade a significant premium over export values as growers remain the largest holders of sorghum and winter planting remains on hold awaiting rain, he said.

While export values have been a little lower over the past week, the world stock situation still leaves potential for a stronger market if planting or weather problems eventuate in either the U.S. or Europe, he said.

Values remained steady in southern Queensland last week with May bids as high as A$156.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane, while central Queensland prices fell late last week to just below A$130.00 a tonne delivered port.
Old crop feed barley values remain steady as the dry weather continues to keep growers reluctant sellers.
Values finished last week at around A$160.00 a tonne Brisbane. However, little tonnage appeared in the market.
New crop price indicators remain uncertain, particularly as areas in Europe await rain for spring planting of barley.

The dry in Spain and France, large suppliers of feed barley to the European Union, meant that new crop indicated prices were currently lower than last season's prices. It was uncertain if the European crop could support values longer-term.

Most international malting barley buyers are covered to July/August this year. Future price direction will be driven by production estimates for Europe and Canada and by planting conditions in Australia to May/June, especially in the south.
New crop indications were currently around A$180.00 port.
Picking of cottonseed was more than 50 percent complete with ginning well underway through Australian cotton growing areas.
On balance the pick has been dry with only a few scattered shower delays and the quality of seed excellent, he said.
"This will go a long way to reinforcing our standing as suppliers of premium quality seed to the export market in particular," he said.

"It is timely ... as over the past few years Australian cottonseed has lost some ground in northern Asian markets as these customers endeavour to generate alternate supplies at cheaper levels, thus sacrificing quality."
With Australian seed still relatively cheap against the U.S., the ability to supply large volumes to Korea, Japan and others would strengthen its position as favoured supplier.

Markets continue to show firmness with both export and domestic interest prevalent. Seed has been trading at the A$140.00-A$145.00 a tonne level ex Darling Downs gin and while very little seed remains uncommitted in central Queensland, seed in Emerald and Biloela was at around A$135.00 ex gin.
With soybean futures volatile, export sales remain strong, fuelling market concern over tight carryout stocks.
Concern over dry weather in Europe have lifted export parity for sunflowers, giving rise to a parallel increase in the domestic price, particularly in central Queensland.
Australian domestic values rose over the past week, with sunflowers finishing at A$305.00 a tonne Darling Downs depots for April 1997 and A$327.00 a tonne Newcastle for April 1997.
Central Queensland new crop black sunflower was around A$262.00-A$267.00 central Queensland depot for May/July 1997.
New crop soybean traded higher at A$417.00 a tonne Brisbane.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
